newsitem.title: UK: British parties both talk tough on EU fish deal.
newsitem.headline: British parties both talk tough on EU fish deal.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major reacted defiantly on Tuesday to a European Union decision to cut fish catches, but opposition leader and election rival Tony Blair said Mickey Mouse could have won a better deal for Britain.

Major, still trailing badly in opinion polls ahead of a national election on May 1, said Britain would not accept the EU plan to cut fishing quotas by 30 percent until the EU solved the problem of so-called "quota hoppers"

"I have not a shred of intention of cutting the British catch until or unless we get a satisfactory agreement on quota hopping," Major told reporters during a campaign visit to the town of Tavistock in western England.

Quota hopping refers to the perfectly legal practice whereby foreign fishermen, mainly Spanish and Dutch, have bought up about 25 percent of the British fishing fleet to gain greater access to EU catch quotas.
Britain, backed only by France, was outvoted on Tuesday when EU fisheries ministers meeting in Luxembourg decided on the 30 percent cuts in catches.
Blair, visiting the south coast resort of Brighton, said the fisheries deal was "yet another failure" for the Conservatives.
"They talk tough and they get nothing done, because they are hopelessly divided," he told reporters.
"A Labour government will get a better deal for the British fishing industry. In my view Mickey Mouse would get a better deal than this lot."
Major's defiant stand allowed him to regain some ground on the Europe issue, which has so far served more to point up divisions in the ruling party.

Ministers earlier unleashed furious attacks on Blair, accusing him of hypocrisy over education policy and naivety over economic plans, and prepared to welcome what are expected to be favourable figures on unemployment to be published on Wednesday.

But at a campaign news conference they were forced to divert their attention from these issues by news that a Conservative vice-chairwoman, Angela Rumbold, was defying Major's policy on the single European currency.
Rumbold, head of the party's candidates department, said in an election address to her south London constituents that she would under no circumstances vote to give up the pound sterling.

"No to more powers for Brussels. No to a single currency. Yes to a referendum before any further steps of constitutional importance are taken," she wrote in direct contradiction of Major's official "wait and see" policy on monetary union.
Blair, whose party leads the Conservatives by 21 points in the latest opinion poll, said Major's party would be "like ferrets in a sack" over Europe if they won on May 1.
Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, said: "The Conservative ship is breaking up. John Major is alone on the bridge and the crew are running for the lifeboats."

The latest opinion poll published by the London Evening Standard newspaper said support for both Labour and the Conservatives was unchanged at 50 and 29 percent respectively compared to a similar poll in mid-March. Backing for the Liberal Democrats rose one point to 15 percent.
